faqs.question: When should I start working with a CPA?
faqs.answer: Anytime — but the best savings happen before December 31. New clients often start with a mid-year review so we can still change withholding, estimates, retirement contributions, and entity decisions.

faqs.question: Do you only prepare returns, or do you plan year-round?
faqs.answer: Both. Compliance is the floor. Most clients stay on a year-round advisory cadence with quarterly check-ins so April is a filing event, not a strategy session.

faqs.question: Can you help with IRS notices, back taxes, or liens?
faqs.answer: Yes. We review the notice, reconstruct filings if needed, and represent you with the IRS or state. Resolution options include installment agreements, penalty relief, and currently-not-collectible status when they apply.

faqs.question: Do you work with clients outside your city?
faqs.answer: Yes. We meet in person at our offices and virtually nationwide. Multi-state returns are a regular part of the practice.

faqs.question: What should I bring to a first consultation?
faqs.answer: Last year’s return if you have it, a list of income sources, any IRS or state letters, and the questions keeping you up at night. We will tell you what else we need before we propose an engagement.

faqs.question: How do you charge?
faqs.answer: Individual and business returns are quoted after we understand complexity. Advisory and resolution work can be a flat project fee or a monthly retainer. We put the fee in writing before we start.

newsPosts.title: Extended hours through April 15
newsPosts.excerpt: Evening and Saturday appointments are open through filing deadline. Book a slot before the calendar fills.
newsPosts.body:
Tax season is here. In addition to weekday hours, Hartwell & Associates will be open selected evenings and Saturdays through April 15 so you can review documents without missing work.

Existing clients can book through the usual advisor. New clients should request a consultation — we still take a limited number of new individual and business returns each season.

blogPosts.title: The small-business deduction checklist we actually use
blogPosts.excerpt: Home office, vehicles, retirement, and the expenses owners forget until the IRS has already closed the year.
blogPosts.body:
Most overpaid tax bills are not about exotic strategies. They are about incomplete books and decisions made after December 31.

Start with a clean profit-and-loss, then walk vehicle use, home office, retirement contributions, health premiums, and estimated payments. If you take an owner draw instead of a reasonable salary from an S-corp, fix that before you file.

Bring this list to your next review. We will tell you what still moves the needle this year and what has to wait until January.
blogPosts.author: Marcus Adeyemi, CPA

blogPosts.title: You received an IRS letter. Here is the first week.
blogPosts.excerpt: Do not ignore it, and do not call the number on the notice in a panic. A calm sequence works better.
blogPosts.body:
Open the envelope. Note the notice number, the tax year, and the deadline. Then send us the PDF. Most letters are math mismatches, missing forms, or identity checks — not audits.

We reply on your behalf, request transcripts when needed, and only escalate to representation if the facts require it. Waiting rarely improves the outcome. Guessing on the phone often makes it worse.
blogPosts.author: Priya Nair, CPA

blogPosts.title: Estimated taxes for freelancers who hate surprises
blogPosts.excerpt: A simple quarterly rhythm so April does not wipe out a good year.
blogPosts.body:
If you receive 1099 income, the IRS expects payments through the year. We set estimates from your current books, not last year’s guess, and we adjust after a strong or slow quarter.

Pair estimates with a retirement contribution plan and an entity review. Plenty of freelancers overpay because they never looked at an S-corp or a SEP IRA until the return was already prepared.
blogPosts.author: Elena Hartwell, CPA
